hints: Notice when $f_{max}$ and $f_{min}$ occur: $f_{max}$ is when the observed star moves fastest toward the observer on Earth and $f_{min}$ is when it moves fastest away.
Connect line-of-sight speed to Doppler shift: larger speed toward gives larger increase in observed frequency, larger speed away gives larger decrease in observed frequency.
Ask what a larger rate of rotation does to the orbital speed $v$ and therefore to the size of the shift $\Delta f$ about the mean frequency for both approach and recession.
walkthrough: Identify the geometry from the diagram: the observer sees the star sometimes moving toward Earth and half an orbit later moving away from Earth.
Recall the Doppler effect for light: motion toward the observer increases observed frequency to $f_{max}$ and motion away decreases it to $f_{min}$.
A larger rate of rotation means a larger orbital speed $v$, so the component of velocity along the line to Earth is larger at both extremes.
Larger approach speed produces a larger blueshift, so the peak observed frequency $f_{max}$ becomes larger than before.
Larger recession speed produces a larger redshift, so the trough observed frequency $f_{min}$ becomes smaller than before.
Therefore $f_{max}$ increases and $f_{min}$ decreases. This is option C.

A.explanation: Both frequencies decreasing would mean a systematic redshift, not a larger approaching speed giving a larger blueshift for $f_{max}$.

B.explanation: A faster approach should increase the blueshifted $f_{max}$, not decrease it, and a faster recession should decrease $f_{min}$.

C.explanation: Faster rotation gives larger line-of-sight speed, so the approaching blueshift is larger and $f_{max}$ rises while the receding redshift is larger and $f_{min}$ falls.

D.explanation: Both frequencies increasing would mean a systematic blueshift, not a larger Doppler spread with more redshift when receding.
